scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Orteke originated in southwestern Kazakhstan and spread across Central Asian nomadic pastoral cultures, including regions of Uzbekistan.
The name joins 'or' (a ditch, hole, or pit trap) with 'teke' (a buck or male mountain goat).

Scholars and ethnographers argue that the practice originated in prehistory, potentially serving ancient shamans as a tool to distract spirits or act as a spirit vessel during therapeutic and healing rites.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Traditionally staged within nomadic encampments and domestic gatherings, orteke serves as an artistic tribute to wildlife, pastoral life, and the rugged mountain ecology inhabited by wild goats.
Beyond its historical associations with shamanic healing, the performance functions as an entertaining and educational medium of communication between adults and children.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The kinetic dance of orteke is performed not by human bodies stepping across a floor, but by mechanical proxy through an articulated puppet operated by a seated musician.
The instrumentalist, known as a küyshi, sits holding a two-stringed dombra.
Strings or threads are fastened to the musician's playing fingers or wrists and run to the puppet, which is mounted on a metal rod over a dauylpaz drum or table.
Watch for goat leaping.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical foundation of orteke is provided by the dombra (or dombyra), the traditional two-stringed Kazakh long-necked plucked lute.

The sound of the plucked strings is acoustically doubled by the percussive impact of the wooden goat striking the skin of a dauylpaz drum, functioning as an integrated self-accompanying percussion system.
Listen for the dombra, dauylpaz, sazsyrnay, shankobyz.

A rapid, resonant plucked lute melody played on the two strings of the dombra, accented by the sharp, intermittent woody clatter and dull tapping of the marionette's hooves landing upon the skin of a dauylpaz drum, occasionally supplemented by the high whistle of the sazsyrnay or the buzzing hum of the shankobyz.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performances occur in intimate or theatrical indoor and outdoor gathering spaces.
The physical apparatus rests upon a wooden table draped with traditional animal skin or fabric decorated with national Kazakh embroidery.
The puppet, historically assembled from dried mountain goat skin stuffed with straw in the Semirechye region, is more universally carved from red birch, walnut, maple, ash, or oak wood.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical figures linked to the master repertoire of orteke melodies include classical küyshis Tattimbet, Bayserke, Shashubay, and Nawryzbay.
In 1935, Kazakh composer and academic Akhmet Kuanovich Zhubanov provided the first detailed modern analysis of the art form.

Within Kazakhstan, construction methods vary regionally; the Semirechye region historically utilized real goat hide filled with straw, while western and central regions favoured carved timber from birch, walnut, ash, and oak.
Orteke descends from ancient Turkic pastoral puppetry and shamanic performance traditions.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: orteke is variant of buz-bazi: Shared tradition of goat-and-lute mechanical puppetry practiced in Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Afghanistan.
orteke is variant of takteke: Kyrgyz tradition where two combatant puppets are manipulated alongside the playing of the komuz.

Level: Level 1. Difficulty of the dance overall: advanced.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Musician sits upright or cross-legged, holding the dombra steady while arms and hands maintain precise tension over the puppet's connecting cords.
Right plucking hand strikes the dombra strings while fingers and wrists flex upward to pull the puppet's attached strings; expert players incorporate left-hand or foot string tethers.
Musician's torso remains relatively steady to anchor the lute and provide leverage for the puppet's string mechanisms.

wardrobe.from_sources: Performances occur in intimate or theatrical indoor and outdoor gathering spaces. The physical apparatus rests upon a wooden table draped with traditional animal skin or fabric decorated with national Kazakh embroidery. The puppet, historically assembled from dried mountain goat skin stuffed with straw in the Semirechye region, is more universally carved from red birch, walnut, maple, ash, or oak wood. The animal features curved horns and flexible joints attached via strings to the performer's digits, mounted firmly above a drum surface via a metal rod. The küyshi typically wears traditional Kazakh dress suited for formal instrumental concerts and community festivals.
